newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks end mixed, high techs dazzle ... again.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks end mixed, high techs dazzle ... again.

text.p: U.S. stocks ended mixed as fresh economic data further stoked inflation fears in the bond market, but the high-technology sector again stole the show and drew avid buying.

"It's a day where techs are up and the rest of the market is languishing. A lot of the big-cap techs that have been strong are staying strong and the former high-flyers that were killed (in the July correction) are coming back on short-covering," said Roy Blumberg of Josephthal Lyon & Ross.
The Dow industrials lost nine to about 5868.
Losers beat gainers 12-11 on heavy NYSE volume of about 396 million shares.
The Nasdaq Composite, which has surged six percent since the start of September, added six to 1212, closer to June 5's all-time high finish of 1249.15.
By comparison, the Dow has risen four percent since September 3, the S&P 500 is up four percent and the Philadelphia Stock Exchange's semiconductor index is up nine percent.
Richard Cripps, chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker, said tech leaders were benefitting from window-dressing.

Bellwether Intel rose 1-3/8 to 97 after touching a fresh 52-week high of 97-1/2 intraday. The stock has climbed 19 percent so far this month, with more buying sparked after Intel's late Monday forecast of higher-than-expected third-quarter revenues.

Software giant Microsoft rose 1-1/4 to 137-3/4, after hitting another new year-high of 138-1/4 earlier. Among other technology issues, Micron rose 1-7/8 to 27-3/8, America Online added 3-1/4 to 33-1/8, Hewlett-Packard rose 1/4 to 48-3/8 and IBM lost one to 123-1/2 after recent strength.
The long bond shed 12/32 to yield 7.05 percent.

Strong housing starts, lower-than-expected weekly jobless claims and an ample rise in the prices paid index of the Philadelphia Federal Reserve's September survey lent more credence to expectations that the Fed may need to raise interest rates at its policy meeting next Tuesday.
August housing starts rose 4.5 percent to a 1.525 million annual rate, the highest level since March 1994. A modest decline had been expected.
The Philadelphia Fed business outlook index fell to 13.9 in September versus 21.5 in August but the closely watched prices paid index surged to 18.0 from 4.6 in August.
Initial claims for unemployment benefits fell to 329,000 in the week ended September 14 from a revised 331,000 the prior week.

"Again, the (stock) market has a lot of resiliency here. You'd think we'd have broader profit-taking given the decline in bonds," Cripps said. "People are afraid to leave the market. They want to get on board here and won't shake out with a bad housing starts number."
Among individual shares, Ethan Allen surged 3-1/8 to 30-5/8 after forecasting first-quarter results would top Street expectations.

Three initial public offerings among Nasdaq's best performers. Cymer Corp soared 43 percent or 4-1/8 to 13-5/8. Cymer makes makes excimer lasers for deep ultraviolet photolithography systems, which make the very small images used in manufacturing advanced semiconductor chips.
Rental Services Corp, which rents out pumps, generators, forklifts and other industrial equipment, rose 5-3/4 points to 21-3/4, or 36 percent at its market debut.
Another IPO, RMH Teleservices, rose 2-1/2 to 15. RMH provides outbound teleservices for insurance and financial services companies.
Blumberg, chief investment strategist at Josephthal, saw little market impact Thursday ahead of Friday's triple witching expiration of September futures and options.
Traders saw an upward bias that might lead to a stronger opening Friday.
The Nasdaq Composite rose 6.38 to 1212.09.
The S&P 500 index rose 1.53 to 683.00.
(Figures official as of 1645 EDT/2045 GMT)
-- Wall Street desk, 212 859 1721
